title: Rethinking User Delight
intro: Teams that set out to “add delight” usually layer effects on top of the product. The result is often slower, less accessible and more frustrating. Calabro goes back to Bill Scott's idea of **interesting moments**.

learn.title: Six misunderstandings
learn.text:
**1.** Skipping the basics
**2.** Confusing good looks with good design
**3.** Misusing design systems
**4.** Over-relying on motion
**5.** Overloading the screen
**6.** Trying to please everyone

If people are forced to wait, guess or reorient mid-flow, no decoration fixes it.

try.q: A team adds animations to a checkout that still has usability problems. Which misunderstanding is this?
try.explain: Surface enhancements on a flow that still fails.

learn.title: Scott's principles
learn.text:
**Keep interactions direct:** show only what's needed, when it's needed.
**Maintain flow:** keep users in context; avoid interruptions.
**Respond with intent:** feedback should match the user's action, “not to entertain, but to reassure and guide.”

Delight comes from well-timed interactions, when things unfold as expected or better.

try.q: What is system feedback for, in Scott's “respond with intent”?
try.explain: Feedback aligns with the user's action.

learn.title: Two animations
learn.text:
Calabro's two examples both use animation and both look polished.

✅ One gives immediate, contextual feedback **as the user types** and prevents errors.
❌ The other interrupts someone who has just found what they were looking for.

Also: Material or Fluent give visual consistency, but consistency is a tool, not the goal.

options: Feedback that appears as the user types
A transition that plays on page load
A banner that slides in over the content
A looping effect that draws the eye
try.explain: It is triggered by the user and prevents errors.

test.q: Where does delight come from, according to the article?
options: Well-timed interactions that go as expected or better
Playful copy and brand illustrations throughout the product
The number of features on each screen
A consistent component library by itself
test.explain: Pacing and responsiveness, not surface flair.

options: Small interaction details that make a system feel responsive
Marketing campaigns that are timed to major product launches
Surprise rewards shown after a purchase

test.q: A team applies Material components everywhere and calls the product delightful. What is missing?
options: A second design system as backup
test.explain: Visual consistency is a tool, not the goal.

test.q: What is the usual result of “adding delight” as effects?
options: Higher task completion and fewer support requests
test.explain: Style for its own sake causes real harm.

test.q: Which is NOT one of the six misunderstandings?
options: Confusing good looks with good design
test.explain: Responding with intent is one of Scott's principles.
